title: The Brain Paradox: One Window Sticker Sold Giant Lawn Signs
description:
Myth vs. Neural Mechanism — Freedman & Fraser (1966): 'Foot-in-the-Door' — How a Tiny 3-Inch Window Sticker Made 76% Put a Monster Billboard on Their Lawn!, grounded in Jonathan L. Freedman, Scott C. Fraser (1966) (Journal of Personality and Social Psychology). Empirical findings show that knock cold on suburban front doors in pristine Palo Alto, California (Freedman & Fraser, *1966 JPSP, Study 2) and show homeowners a photograph of a massive, poorly lettered, view-blocking billboard reading 'DRIVE CAREFULLY' that your crew wants to dig into their manicured front lawn for a week: understandably, 83.3% refuse — only 16.7% say YES*.

Follow-up physiological and behavioral evidence demonstrates: Now rewind TWO WEEKS EARLIER: a completely different volunteer stops by ONE group of houses and asks a tiny, almost effortless favor — 'Would you put this little 3-inch square "Be a Safe Driver" sticker in the corner of your car or house window?' Almost everyone says sure.

Primary Peer-Reviewed Sources:
- Jonathan L. Freedman, Scott C. Fraser (1966). Compliance without pressure: The foot-in-the-door technique. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/h0023552
- Patricia Pliner, Heather Hart, Joanne Kohl, Dory Saari (1974). Compliance without pressure: Some further data on the foot-in-the-door technique. Journal of Experimental Social Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1016/0022-1031(74)90053-5
- Malgorzata Gamian-Wilk, Dariusz Dolinski (2020). The Foot-in-the-Door Phenomenon 40 and 50 Years Later: A Direct Replication of the Original Freedman and Fraser Study in Poland and in Ukraine. Psychological Reports. https://doi.org/10.1177/0033294119872208
